goals.title: Reduce a matrix to $R$ and read the special solutions
goals.description:
The learner can reduce a matrix to its reduced row echelon form $R$ and read the special solutions from it. Go on from $U$ as in Gauss–Jordan elimination in U2: divide each pivot row by its pivot and clear the entries above each pivot. $R$ has pivots $1$ with zeros above and below them. Where the pivot rows meet the pivot columns, $R$ holds an identity matrix $I$; the free columns hold a part $F$, and zero rows come last. When the pivot columns come first, $R = \begin{bmatrix} I & F \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$, and $R\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ says that the pivot variables equal $-F$ times the free variables. So the special solutions are the columns of the nullspace matrix

$$
N = \begin{bmatrix} -F \\ I \end{bmatrix}
$$

When the pivot columns are not the first ones, each special solution still holds $-1$ times a free column of $R$ in its pivot variables, and $1$ and $0$ in its free variables.

For the echelon matrix $U$ of the goal on pivots and rank, divide row 2 by its pivot $-3$, then add the new row 2 to row 1:

$$
U = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & -3 & 3 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \to R = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
$$

Then

$$
F = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 5 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad N = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & -5 \\ 1 & -2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
$$

The columns of $N$ are the special solutions $\mathbf{s}_1$ and $\mathbf{s}_2$ found by back substitution, now read off without any substitution.

At 19:03 in Lecture 7, follow elimination upward, the division by the pivots, the identity in the pivot rows and columns, and how $-F$ appears in the special solutions. At 40:31, see the same for a matrix with one free column.

goals.title: Write the complete solution $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}_p + \mathbf{x}_n$
goals.description:
The learner can decide for which $\mathbf{b}$ the system $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ is solvable and write its complete solution $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}_p + \mathbf{x}_n$. Eliminate on the augmented matrix $\begin{bmatrix} A & \mathbf{b} \end{bmatrix}$, doing every row operation to $\mathbf{b}$ as well. A zero row of $U$ turns into a condition on $\mathbf{b}$: the combination of the rows that gave the zero row must give $0$ in $\mathbf{b}$ too. When the conditions hold, set all free variables to $0$ and solve for the pivot variables; in $\begin{bmatrix} R & \mathbf{d} \end{bmatrix}$ they are the entries of $\mathbf{d}$. This particular solution $\mathbf{x}_p$ solves $A\mathbf{x}_p = \mathbf{b}$. Every $\mathbf{x}_n$ in the nullspace can be added, since $A(\mathbf{x}_p + \mathbf{x}_n) = \mathbf{b} + \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{b}$, and every solution $\mathbf{x}$ has this form, because $A(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_p) = \mathbf{0}$. So the complete solution is $\mathbf{x}_p$ plus all combinations of the special solutions, with no free constant in front of $\mathbf{x}_p$. The solutions are the nullspace shifted by $\mathbf{x}_p$, which misses $\mathbf{0}$ when $\mathbf{b} \neq \mathbf{0}$.

For the matrix $A$ of the goal on pivots and rank and $\mathbf{b} = (b_1, b_2, b_3)$, the two steps of elimination leave $b_3 + b_2 - 2b_1$ beside the zero row, so the system is solvable exactly when $b_3 = 2b_1 - b_2$. For $\mathbf{b} = (2, 1, 3)$ the condition holds, and

$$
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 2 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & -5 & 7 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 & 6 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \to \begin{bmatrix} R & \mathbf{d} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 & 5 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
$$

With $x_3 = x_4 = 0$ the pivot variables are $x_1 = 3$ and $x_2 = 1$, so

$$
\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}_p + \mathbf{x}_n = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + c_1\begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + c_2\begin{bmatrix} -5 \\ -2 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}
$$

This also writes the solution family that U1 showed only by two witnesses: $x + y = 1$ and $2x + 2y = 2$ have the complete solution $(1, 0) + c(-1, 1)$. The figure shows it as the nullspace line $x + y = 0$ shifted by $\mathbf{x}_p = (1, 0)$.

goals.title: Tell from the rank how many solutions $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ has
goals.description:
The learner can use the rank $r$ of an $m \times n$ matrix to tell whether $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ has no, exactly one or infinitely many solutions. Always $r \leq m$ and $r \leq n$, because each row and each column holds at most one pivot. Full column rank $r = n$ leaves no free variables: $N(A) = \mathbf{Z}$, $R$ has $I$ above $m - n$ zero rows, and there is exactly one solution when $\mathbf{b}$ is in $C(A)$ and none otherwise. Full row rank $r = m$ leaves no zero rows: $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ is solvable for every $\mathbf{b}$, and there are $n - m$ free variables, so infinitely many solutions when $n > m$. When $r = m = n$, $A$ is square and invertible, $R = I$, and there is exactly one solution for every $\mathbf{b}$. When $r < m$ and $r < n$, some $\mathbf{b}$ give no solution and the others infinitely many.

For example,

$$
B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad C = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -3 \end{bmatrix}
$$

$B$ has the pivots $1$ and $2$, so $r = n = 2 < m = 3$: $N(B) = \mathbf{Z}$, and $B\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ has at most one solution. $C$ has the pivots $2$ and $1$, so $r = m = 2 < n = 3$: $C\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ is solvable for every $\mathbf{b}$, with one free variable. The matrix $A$ of the earlier goals has $r = 2$, less than $m = 3$ and $n = 4$, so its system has no solution unless $b_3 = 2b_1 - b_2$, and then infinitely many.

At 24:30 in Lecture 8, follow the bounds on the rank and the case of full column rank with its example. From 34:55, see the case of full row rank, the square invertible case and the summary of all four cases.

examData.taskContent:
Items 1 to 3 use

$$
A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & -2 & 0 \\ -2 & -4 & 6 & -4 \\ 1 & 5 & 0 & q \end{bmatrix}
$$

1. Eliminate $A$ to an echelon matrix $U$ and show the multipliers. Say what happens in column 3. For which $q$ does $A$ have rank $2$, and what is its rank for every other $q$? Name the pivot columns and the free columns in both cases. For the $q$ of rank $2$, write row 3 of $A$ as a combination of rows 1 and 2, read from your elimination steps. Why do $A$ and $U$ have the same nullspace?

2. Take the $q$ of rank $2$. Name the pivot variables and the free variables, find the special solutions and describe $N(A)$ with them. How many special solutions are there for every other $q$, and which vector is it?

3. For the $q$ of rank $2$, reduce $U$ to $R$. Give $F$, read the nullspace matrix $N$ from $F$, and say how its columns are related to item 2. Next, a matrix $\widetilde{R}$ with two rows is in reduced row echelon form, has no zero row and has the special solutions $(3, 1, 0, 0)$ and $(-4, 0, 5, 1)$. Which columns of $\widetilde{R}$ are its pivot columns? Find $\widetilde{R}$.

Give each reason in one sentence that names the rows, columns or variables of the task. Show your work. Method points follow through from the earlier values you show, and a single arithmetic slip is charged once.
examData.solutionContent:
1. The multipliers are $\ell_{21} = -2$ and $\ell_{31} = 1$: adding $2$ times row 1 to row 2 and subtracting row 1 from row 3 gives the rows $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 2 & 2 & -4 \end{bmatrix}$ and $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 2 & 2 & q \end{bmatrix}$. With $\ell_{32} = 1$, subtracting the new row 2 from row 3 leaves $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 & q + 4 \end{bmatrix}$. Column 3 has no nonzero entry left in row 3, so elimination goes on to column 4 in the same row:

   $$
   U = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 2 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & q + 4 \end{bmatrix}
   $$

   The only candidate for a third pivot is $q + 4$. For $q \neq -4$ the pivots are $1$, $2$ and $q + 4$, the rank is $3$, the pivot columns are 1, 2 and 4, and column 3 is free. For $q = -4$ the third row is zero, the rank is $2$, the pivot columns are 1 and 2, and columns 3 and 4 are free. Row 3 of $A$ is then row 1 plus the new row 2, which is row 2 plus $2$ times row 1, so row 3 is $3$ times row 1 plus row 2: $3\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & -2 & 0 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} -2 & -4 & 6 & -4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 5 & 0 & -4 \end{bmatrix}$. $A$ and $U$ have the same nullspace, because the three row operations (adding $2$ times row 1 to row 2, subtracting row 1 from row 3, subtracting the new row 2 from row 3) can each be undone, so $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ and $U\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ have the same solutions.

2. For $q = -4$ the pivot variables are $x_1$ and $x_2$, the free variables $x_3$ and $x_4$. With $x_3 = 1$ and $x_4 = 0$, row 2 of $U$ gives $2x_2 + 2 = 0$, so $x_2 = -1$, and row 1 gives $x_1 = -3x_2 + 2 = 5$. With $x_3 = 0$ and $x_4 = 1$, $2x_2 - 4 = 0$ gives $x_2 = 2$ and $x_1 = -3x_2 = -6$. So $\mathbf{s}_1 = (5, -1, 1, 0)$ and $\mathbf{s}_2 = (-6, 2, 0, 1)$, and $N(A)$ contains exactly the combinations $c_1\mathbf{s}_1 + c_2\mathbf{s}_2$. For every other $q$ the only free variable is $x_3$, so there is $n - r = 4 - 3 = 1$ special solution: row 3 forces $x_4 = 0$, and then $x_3 = 1$ gives $\mathbf{s}_1 = (5, -1, 1, 0)$ again.

3. Divide row 2 of $U$ by its pivot $2$ to get $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix}$, then subtract $3$ times it from row 1:

   $$
   R = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -5 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad F = \begin{bmatrix} -5 & 6 \\ 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad N = \begin{bmatrix} -F \\ I \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & -6 \\ -1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
   $$

   The columns of $N$ are $\mathbf{s}_1$ and $\mathbf{s}_2$ of item 2. In $\widetilde{R}$ the free variables are those where the special solutions hold $1$ and $0$, namely $x_2$ and $x_4$, so columns 1 and 3 are the pivot columns. In the pivot variables $x_1$ and $x_3$ each special solution holds $-1$ times the matching free column of $\widetilde{R}$, so free column 2 is $(-3, 0)$ and free column 4 is $(4, -5)$:

   $$
   \widetilde{R} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -3 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -5 \end{bmatrix}
   $$

   Check: $\widetilde{R}$ times $(3, 1, 0, 0)$ and times $(-4, 0, 5, 1)$ gives $\mathbf{0}$.

A $U$ without this statement, or one that gives column 3 a pivot, does not earn the point.

examData.taskContent:
1. Let

   $$
   A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -2 & 4 \\ 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 1 & -4 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
   $$

   Eliminate on $\begin{bmatrix} A & \mathbf{b} \end{bmatrix}$ with $\mathbf{b} = (b_1, b_2, b_3)$ and find the condition on $\mathbf{b}$ for $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ to be solvable. For $\mathbf{b} = (4, 1, 5)$, find the particular solution with the free variable $0$ and the complete solution. Say in one sentence why every vector of your family solves the system and why every solution belongs to it. Describe the set of all solutions in one sentence and say why it is not a subspace. Which solution has the first component $0$? Finally give a right-hand side for which $(1, 1, 1)$ is a solution, and write its complete solution with $(1, 1, 1)$ as the particular solution.

2. Answer the following questions.

   (a) Why can no $4 \times 6$ matrix have rank $5$?

   (b) A $5 \times 3$ matrix $M$ has rank $3$. Describe $N(M)$ and $R$, and say how many solutions $M\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ can have.

   (c) A $2 \times 4$ matrix $K$ has rank $2$. For which $\mathbf{b}$ is $K\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ solvable, and how many free variables are there?

   (d) For the matrix $A$ of item 1, give $r$, $m$ and $n$, name the case, and give one $\mathbf{b}$ without a solution.

   (e) For which $t$ does

   $$
   B = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ -4 & t \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
   $$

   have rank $1$? For every other $t$, what is $N(B)$, and how many solutions can $B\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ have?

   (f) A $4 \times 4$ matrix has rank $4$. What are $R$ and its nullspace, how many solutions does each system with this matrix have, and which word of U2 describes the matrix?

Give each reason in one sentence that names the rows, columns, pivots or sizes of the task. Show your work. Method points follow through from the earlier values you show, and a single arithmetic slip is charged once.
examData.solutionContent:
1. Subtract $\frac{1}{2}$ of row 1 from row 2 and from row 3:

   $$
   \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -2 & 4 & b_1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & b_2 - \frac{1}{2}b_1 \\ 0 & -3 & -3 & b_3 - \frac{1}{2}b_1 \end{bmatrix}
   $$

   Adding $3$ times the new row 2 to row 3 leaves the zero row with $b_3 + 3b_2 - 2b_1$ beside it, so the system is solvable exactly when $2b_1 - 3b_2 - b_3 = 0$. The rows show the same: row 3 of $A$ is $2$ times row 1 minus $3$ times row 2. For $\mathbf{b} = (4, 1, 5)$ the condition holds: $8 - 3 - 5 = 0$. The pivot columns are 1 and 2, so $x_3$ is free. With $x_3 = 0$, row 2 gives $x_2 = 1 - 2 = -1$, and row 1 gives $2x_1 + 2 = 4$, so dividing by the pivot $2$ gives $x_1 = 1$ and $\mathbf{x}_p = (1, -1, 0)$. The special solution has $x_3 = 1$: $x_2 = -1$ and $2x_1 + 2 + 4 = 0$, so $x_1 = -3$ and $\mathbf{s} = (-3, -1, 1)$. The complete solution is

   $$
   \mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + c\begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}
   $$

   for every number $c$. Each of these solves the system, because $A(\mathbf{x}_p + c\mathbf{s}) = \mathbf{b} + \mathbf{0}$. Every solution $\mathbf{x}$ belongs to the family, because $A(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_p) = \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{0}$, so $\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_p$ lies in $N(A)$, the line of multiples of $\mathbf{s}$. The solutions form the line through $(1, -1, 0)$ parallel to that nullspace line. It misses $\mathbf{0}$, since $A\mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0} \neq \mathbf{b}$, so it is no subspace. The first component $1 - 3c$ is $0$ for $c = \frac{1}{3}$, which gives $\mathbf{x} = (0, -\frac{4}{3}, \frac{1}{3})$. For $(1, 1, 1)$ take $\mathbf{b} = A(1, 1, 1) = (4, 4, -4)$, which satisfies $8 - 12 + 4 = 0$. Its complete solution is $(1, 1, 1) + c(-3, -1, 1)$: any one solution can serve as $\mathbf{x}_p$, and the nullspace part stays the same.

2. (a) Each pivot needs its own row, and a $4 \times 6$ matrix has only $4$ rows, so its rank is at most $4$. (b) For $M$, $r = n = 3$: there are no free variables, $N(M) = \mathbf{Z}$, $R$ is the $3 \times 3$ identity above two zero rows, and $M\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ has exactly one solution when $\mathbf{b}$ is in $C(M)$ and none otherwise. (c) For $K$, $r = m = 2$: there are no zero rows, so $K\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ is solvable for every $\mathbf{b}$ in $\mathbf{R}^2$, with $n - m = 2$ free variables and infinitely many solutions. (d) The matrix $A$ of item 1 has $r = 2$, $m = 3$ and $n = 3$, so $r < m$ and $r < n$: some $\mathbf{b}$ have no solution and the others infinitely many. The right-hand side $(1, 0, 0)$ has none, since $2 \cdot 1 - 0 - 0 = 2 \neq 0$.

   (e) For $B$, adding $2$ times row 1 to row 2 gives $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & t - 4 \end{bmatrix}$, and subtracting $\frac{1}{2}$ of row 1 from row 3 gives a zero row. So the rank is $1$ exactly for $t = 4$, when the second column is $-1$ times the first. For $t \neq 4$ the rank is $r = n = 2$: $N(B) = \mathbf{Z}$, and $B\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ has exactly one solution for $\mathbf{b}$ in $C(B)$ and none for the others. (f) A $4 \times 4$ matrix of rank $4$ has $R = I$ and the nullspace $\mathbf{Z}$, each system with it has exactly one solution, and the matrix is invertible.
